A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bandit optimal transport work and EntUCB algorithms, despite the revised title and broader positioning. The complete documents, including Appendices A–H, provide readable text, equations and algorithm descriptions sufficient for comparison.

before.justification: v1 presents algorithms, analytical regret bounds and proofs, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its new logistics, option-pricing and control examples are mathematical illustrations, not reported empirical investigations.

M1.justification: The Fourier/RLS/entropy EntUCB backbone remains, but v2 Appendix D.2 introduces a generalized procedure using a barrier penalty Q_epsilon and a schedule determined by its approximation rate. Under the revised coefficient-decay assumption, basis-truncation EntUCB also changes its prescribed order from ceil(t^(1/(2q+1))) to ceil(t^(1/(q+1))).

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or performs training or evaluation on concrete tasks. The additional application examples and theoretical problem classes in v2 do not constitute evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. OFUL and kernel-bandit methods serve as theoretical reference points, not tested baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an experimental evaluation protocol, data splits, training budgets or testing procedures. Changes to analytical algorithm schedules are methodological and theoretical changes.

E4.justification: Neither version contains ablations, robustness tests or empirical supplementary analyses. The new application examples in v2 Appendix C.3 explain possible uses without testing them.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates or significance tests. Their confidence sets and high-probability bounds are components of the theoretical analysis.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance, empirical rankings or experimental result entries. The revised analytical regret rates and added mathematical guarantees are assessed under T1.

T1.justification: v2 extends the Kantorovich bound from Lipschitz to Hölder costs and adds the general bilinear result in Theorem D.3. Assumption 5.1 and Lemma 5.2 replace the absolute-coefficient treatment with squared-coefficient tails, changing the nonparametric rate from O-tilde(T^((q+1)/(2q+1))) to O-tilde(T^((q+2)/(2q+2))) under the revised assumption. Kolmogorov-width and Sobolev arguments are added. v1's standalone entropic-regret results and RKHS specialization are omitted.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes the first regret analysis for both stochastic Kantorovich and entropic OT. v2 centers its contribution on linear bandits beyond inner-product spaces, with Kantorovich OT as the principal example, and claims a conditional generalization to other bilinear objectives. It also adds a Sobolev-related guarantee and revises the advertised nonparametric rate.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion through logistics and pricing examples, an occupation-measure interpretation of reinforcement learning, and approximation-rate conditions for general bilinear learning. It distinguishes sufficient conditions from unresolved necessity questions and explains that basis regularity concerns the Fourier-transformed cost. The numerical implementation, unknown-marginal and Monge limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: Computational documentation is reduced: v1 Appendix G.1.1 gives explicit Sinkhorn updates and primal-plan recovery instructions, which v2 omits. Both versions leave implementation of the optimistic optimization step unresolved and provide no executable implementation, hardware or timing information.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts from an OT-specific learning contribution to a broader limitation of existing linear-bandit theory. New connections to Gamma-convergence, Kolmogorov widths, functional approximation and entropy-regularized control bring substantive additional references, including Carlier et al. (2017), Kolmogorov, Hu et al. (2025) and Neu et al. (2017).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The separate related-work section is redistributed, and the main narrative now separates algorithm design, trajectory-dependent regret and worst-case regret. Basis-truncation material moves into the main text, while Appendices C–E are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v1's single-column article becomes a two-column main text and bibliography with wide single-column appendices, running headers and substantially reformatted equations. Algorithm blocks gain numbered lines, and Algorithm 2 moves from the appendix into Section 5. Neither version contains empirical figures or result tables.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies the distinction between trajectory-dependent and worst-case guarantees and repairs a specific mathematical inconsistency: v1 Theorem E.8 identifies an absolute coefficient sum with an L2 norm, whereas v2 uses squared-coefficient tails. These improve clarity and the approximation argument. The gains are tempered by reduced coverage of entropic/RKHS variants and computational details. The new general theorem also has an unresolved gap: its proof uses an unweighted finite-time approximation bound although Assumption D.2 supplies an asymptotic bound with a parameter-dependent factor b.
